ConocoPhillips fell 0.86% today to $126.43, extending a sharp two-week decline of 6.4%. The primary driver is a collapse in oil prices: U.S. crude has tumbled to $107 per barrel from over $141 two weeks ago, a drop of roughly 24%. This crash stems directly from a wave of diplomatic developments—reports that Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz (a critical chokepoint for global oil) within a week if the U.S. eases military pressure, combined with hopes that Saudi Arabia will restart a damaged pipeline. These signals have convinced traders that supply disruptions may ease, reducing the scarcity premium that had been pushing oil prices higher.

Oil majors like this one live or die on the price per barrel; when crude falls this steeply, their profits shrink immediately. The market is now pricing in a scenario where Middle Eastern tensions de-escalate through diplomacy rather than conflict, fundamentally weakening the bull case for energy stocks that had benefited from geopolitical risk premiums over the past weeks.
